No matching passages were provided, so this follows general coffee-board practice.
**Do today:** Check the underside of young leaves for yellow-orange rust spots.
**Spray:** 0.5% Bordeaux mixture (1 kg copper sulphate + 1 kg lime in 200 L water), covering the lower leaf surface.
**Timing:** Before the south-west monsoon, around May after the blossom and backing showers, so new leaves are protected before the rains.
**Prevent:** Keep balanced shade and good nutrition; repeat a spray after the monsoon.

April and May are the crucial months when leaf rust spreads from older to young leaves, so a 0.5% Bordeaux mixture spray should be given during this period, sprayed on the lower surface of the leaves.

**Do today:** Look for rust spots on the underside of older leaves and plan the spray before new leaves get infected.
**Spray:** Freshly prepared 0.5% Bordeaux mixture on the lower surface of the leaves.
**Timing:** April-May, the most crucial months for rust spreading from older leaves to young tissue, especially where shade is thin after shade regulation. In areas with very thin shade, rust can build up already in February-March and a 0.5% Bordeaux (or systemic fungicide) spray may be needed then.
**Prevent:** Keep adequate overhead shade during the monsoon; thin or no shade favours rust.
Documents used: coffee_cultivation_guide.pdf (p.21, p.14).

**Do today:** Check where the orange powdery rust spots are: they form on the underside of the leaf.
**Spray:** Direct the Bordeaux mixture to the lower surface of the leaves, where the rust spores develop; good coverage of the underside matters most.
**Timing:** Pre-monsoon and post-monsoon sprays.
**Prevent:** Maintain shade and nutrition.

Bordeaux mixture should be sprayed on the lower surface of the leaves.

**Do today:** Prepare fresh Bordeaux mixture (not the previous day's).
**Spray:** For leaf rust, spray uniformly only on the lower portion (underside) of the leaves. Only for black rot (1% Bordeaux) are both the upper and lower surfaces covered.
**Timing:** Pre-monsoon (April-May), when rust spreads to young leaves.
**Prevent:** Do not add urea, fertilizers, micro-nutrients, insecticides or hormones to the mixture.
Documents used: coffee_cultivation_guide.pdf (p.21 and Annexure).

**Spray:** The passages give a volume only for the systemic fungicide alternative: 7-8 barrels per hectare (160 g Bayleton 25 WP or 400 ml Contaf 5EC in 200 L of water). They do not state how many barrels of Bordeaux mixture cover a hectare, so follow the label or ask your extension officer.
**Timing:** Systemic sprays are used during the break in the monsoon when Bordeaux is avoided.

**Spray:** Do not mix urea into Bordeaux mixture. Mixing fertilizers into copper sprays can reduce the fungicide's effect and may damage leaves. Apply urea separately as a soil or foliar application.
**Prevent:** Use only freshly prepared Bordeaux without additives.

No. Adding urea to the Bordeaux mixture is a bad practice that should be avoided, because it leads to loss of nitrogen as ammonia and lowers the efficiency of the spray.

**Do today:** Prepare plain Bordeaux mixture only.
**Spray:** Do not add urea. The guide says not to add any foreign ingredients to Bordeaux mixture, such as urea, phosphatic fertilizers, micro-nutrients, insecticides, pesticides or hormones. Use only freshly prepared mixture, sprayed on the lower leaf surface for rust.
**Timing:** April-May for the pre-monsoon rust spray.
**Prevent:** Apply fertilizers separately.
Documents used: coffee_cultivation_guide.pdf (Annexure, p.21).

Leaf rust is favoured by warm temperatures (about 20-25 C), high humidity and leaf wetness from rain or dew, which let the spores germinate; it builds up during the monsoon and after it. Heavy crop load and poor nutrition make plants more susceptible.
**Prevent:** Maintain shade and nutrition, and spray before and after the monsoon.
Documents used: none (general practice).

Humid, cool weather with wind from May to November with intermittent showers and sunshine, and dry weather from December to March with cloudy, misty weather and drizzle in February-March favour the early appearance of leaf rust. Thin or no overhead shade during the south-west monsoon is also a favourable factor.

**Do today:** Watch for rust where shade is thin.
**Spray:** In thin-shade areas where rust appears early, spray 0.5% Bordeaux mixture or a systemic fungicide (Contaf or Bayleton).
**Timing:** Conditions favouring early rust: humid, cool, windy weather from May to November with intermittent showers and sunshine; dry weather from December to March with cloudy, misty weather and drizzle in February-March; and thin or no overhead shade during the south-west monsoon.
**Prevent:** Keep overhead shade; estates above 3500 feet are generally not affected in February-March.
Documents used: coffee_cultivation_guide.pdf (p.14).

**Spray:** A post-monsoon spray of 0.5% Bordeaux mixture or a recommended systemic fungicide on the underside of the leaves.

**Spray:** A post-monsoon Bordeaux mixture (0.5%) or a systemic fungicide such as Contaf or Bayleton.

**Prevent:** Maintain shade.

**Do today:** Buy good-quality spray lime (not agricultural lime).
**Spray:** The passages give only part of the recipe: with 100% pure spray lime only 300 g is needed for 0.5% Bordeaux mixture, but because market lime is often impure, use up to 1 kg of spray lime. Do not use agricultural lime. The amount of copper sulphate and the mixing steps are not in the passages; follow the guide's annexure.
**Timing:** Use only freshly prepared mixture, never the previous day's.
**Prevent:** Add nothing else (no urea, fertilizers, insecticides or hormones).

For organic farms, plant rust-resistant varieties, keep good shade and balanced organic nutrition, remove heavily infected leaves, and use copper-based sprays (Bordeaux mixture), which are usually permitted in organic certification within limits.
Documents used: none (general practice).
The main control measure should be the use of rust-resistant cultivars, integrated with cultural, biological and chemical control using active principles permitted by organic certifiers.

**Do today:** Plan to replace susceptible plants.
**Spray:** Where needed, use only copper products allowed by your organic certifier.
**Timing:** Integrate measures through the year.
**Prevent:** Prioritise rust-resistant cultivars as the main control measure, and integrate cultural, biological and chemical control permitted by certifiers. Keep balanced nutrition (nitrogen and potassium) because nutrient imbalance favours rust; note that shading can increase rust progress.
Documents used: Strategies for Coffee Leaf Rust Management in Organic Crop Systems (Agronomy 2021).

**Do today:** Remove badly spotted seedlings.
**Spray:** A copper fungicide (e.g. copper oxychloride) or a recommended fungicide such as carbendazim at label dose.
**Prevent:** Provide partial shade, avoid overexposure to sun and keep seedlings well nourished, especially with nitrogen and potassium.

Bordeaux mixture was found best for managing Cercospora leaf spot, followed by Trichoderma and cow urine; the disease is worse with nitrogen and potassium deficiency and over-exposure to sunlight, so spray Bordeaux mixture and keep the seedlings well nourished and not over-exposed to sun.

**Do today:** Check tender leaves of nursery seedlings for brown eye spots.
**Spray:** Indofil M-45 (5 g per litre of water) or Bavistin (1 g per litre).
**Timing:** Spray when seedlings are in the nursery bags.
**Prevent:** Provide overhead pandal shade until the regular monsoon starts; Bordeaux mixture was also the best eco-friendly treatment in field trials.
Documents used: coffee_cultivation_guide.pdf (p.17); Ecofriendly management of Cercospora leaf spot (RJOAS 2022).

Cercospora (brown eye spot) is more common on young plants and nursery seedlings, on plants exposed to full sun without shade, and on plants that are poorly nourished, especially low in nitrogen, or stressed by drought.
**Prevent:** Provide shade, balanced fertilizer and adequate water.
Documents used: none (general practice).
Cercospora leaf spot is more problematic in newly established coffee orchards and in fields with plant nutrition deficiency, particularly nitrogen and potassium, and with over-exposure to sunlight.

**Do today:** Check newly planted fields and nursery plants first.
**Spray:** Bordeaux mixture gave the best eco-friendly control in field trials, with Trichoderma and cow urine close behind.
**Prevent:** The disease is worse in newly established orchards, in plants deficient in nutrients (especially nitrogen and potassium) and in plants over-exposed to sunlight, so keep nutrition balanced and provide shade.
Documents used: Ecofriendly management of Cercospora leaf spot (RJOAS 2022).

Brown eye spot shows as small round brown spots with a pale grey or whitish centre and a yellow ring (halo) around them, giving an 'eye' appearance. Severe spotting causes leaves to yellow and fall.
Documents used: none (general practice).
On the top leaf surface, lesions begin as yellow (chlorotic) patches that become deep brown and necrotic; many spots have a yellow halo around the edges and a discoloured, light centre.

**Do today:** Inspect the upper surface of leaves.
**Symptoms:** Lesions start as yellow (chlorotic) patches that turn deep brown and necrotic; many spots have a yellow halo and a light, discoloured centre where the fungus sporulates. The halo is caused by the toxin cercosporin.
**Spray:** Bordeaux mixture was the best eco-friendly treatment in field trials.
**Prevent:** Avoid nitrogen and potassium deficiency and over-exposure to sun.
Documents used: Ecofriendly management of Cercospora leaf spot (RJOAS 2022).

On berries, brown eye spot causes dark, sunken, irregular brown blotches (berry blotch), often on the side facing the sun, as the berries develop after flowering. Affected berries may ripen early or drop.
Documents used: none (general practice).

Fruit symptoms typically appear about 90 days after flowering. On green berries there are irregularly shaped brown, sunken lesions surrounded by a purple halo, and infected red cherries have large dark areas of sunken flesh.

**Do today:** Inspect berries about three months after flowering.
**Symptoms:** Fruit symptoms typically appear 90 days after flowering. Green berries show irregularly shaped brown, sunken lesions surrounded by a purple halo; red cherries show large dark areas of sunken flesh, and damaged fruit can be attacked by other fungi.
**Spray:** Bordeaux mixture gave the best eco-friendly control in trials.
**Prevent:** Keep nutrition balanced.
Documents used: Ecofriendly management of Cercospora leaf spot (RJOAS 2022).

Documents used: none (general practice).
Bordeaux mixture was the most effective, with the lowest disease index after four sprays at 20-day intervals, followed by Trichoderma and cow urine.

**Spray:** Bordeaux mixture was the most effective eco-friendly treatment, probably because copper is toxic to the pathogen; it gave the lowest disease index and the slowest disease progress. Trichoderma and cow urine followed and were statistically at par at the last observation.
**Prevent:** Integrate these low-cost treatments.
Documents used: Ecofriendly management of Cercospora leaf spot (RJOAS 2022).

The leaf miner moth lays eggs on the leaf; the larvae tunnel inside the leaf, eating the green tissue and leaving brown, dried patches (mines). Heavily mined leaves drop, reducing photosynthesis and yield.
Documents used: none (general practice).

The larvae feed on the mesophyll of the coffee leaves, creating mines that cause necrosis and reduce the photosynthetic leaf surface, lowering the photosynthetic rate and productivity; the damage also includes defoliation.

**Do today:** Look for brown mined patches on the leaves.
**Damage:** The larvae feed inside the leaf on the mesophyll (palisade parenchyma), creating mines that cause necrosis, reduce the photosynthetic surface and lead to defoliation and lower fruit production.
**Prevent:** Integrated control: resistant cultivars, bio-extracts, pheromones; chemical control is used but resistance to insecticides has been reported.
Documents used: A Comprehensive Review of the Coffee Leaf Miner (Insects 2021).

In severe outbreaks the leaf miner can cause heavy defoliation and yield losses of roughly 30-50% or more, especially in dry seasons and in unshaded plantations.
Documents used: none (general practice).
Estimated losses in neotropical producing countries can reach up to 87% of coffee productivity, depending on the season, and defoliation can reach up to 75%.

**Damage level:** The coffee leaf miner causes losses ranging from 30-70% and impairs grain quality; in neotropical countries losses can reach up to 87% of productivity, and defoliation up to 75%. High infestations cause losses above 50% in Brazil and Colombia, 20-40% in Puerto Rico and about 12% in Mexico.
**Prevent:** Integrated pest management with resistant cultivars and biological control.
Documents used: A Comprehensive Review of the Coffee Leaf Miner (Insects 2021).

Newly hatched larvae are translucent whitish and take on a greenish yellow tone as they develop; the last instar is about 4-5 mm long, flattened, segmented with 11 segments and yellowish, with a flat head and chewing mouthparts.

The retrieved passages describe the leaf miner's damage and losses but not what the larva looks like: they say only that the larvae feed inside the leaf mesophyll, causing necrosis and defoliation. Ask your extension officer for identification help.
**Prevent:** Integrated control with resistant cultivars, biological control and bio-pesticides.
Documents used: A Comprehensive Review of the Coffee Leaf Miner (Insects 2021).

Chemical control has harmful effects on human health and the environment and selects resistant insect populations, which is why integrated pest management tools are being developed.

**Problems:** Chemical pesticides harm human health and the environment and select resistant insect populations; resistance has been reported for most insecticides currently used. Markets are also moving towards more sustainable, pesticide-free coffee.
**Prevent:** Use integrated pest management: resistant cultivars, biological control, nano-biopesticides, bio-extracts and pheromones.
Documents used: A Comprehensive Review of the Coffee Leaf Miner (Insects 2021).

**Options:** Resistant cultivars, biological control, nano-biopesticide products and other integrated approaches; the review also discusses bio-extracts, nanotechnology, pheromones and tolerant cultivars.
**Prevent:** Reduce reliance on chemicals because resistance to insecticides has been reported.
Documents used: A Comprehensive Review of the Coffee Leaf Miner (Insects 2021).

**Prevent:** Yes. Conserving the natural enemies already present, by diversifying the coffee farm, is very important; shade regulation and pruning also reduce leaf miner. Prefer neem kernel extract or other plant-based extracts and IPM tools over broad chemical sprays, which harm health and the environment and select resistance.
Documents used: coffee pest management notes; A Comprehensive Review of the Coffee Leaf Miner (Insects 2021).

White stem borer beetles usually emerge in two flight periods: around April-May (pre-monsoon) and again around October-December (post-monsoon), and are active on bright sunny days.
Documents used: none (general practice).

White stem borer beetles attain adulthood and emerge in large numbers during April-May and October-December; in very favourable conditions they can emerge throughout the year except during the monsoon.

**Do today:** Plan control before the flight periods.
**Timing:** Adults emerge in large numbers in April-May and October-December; under favourable conditions they can emerge throughout the year except in the monsoon, and one brood can reach adulthood in February-March. Rain followed by bright sunshine triggers emergence.
**Prevent:** Trace and uproot infested plants, smoothen stems and apply 10% lime, maintain optimum shade, and install 25 pheromone traps per hectare where incidence is high.
Documents used: coffee_cultivation_guide.pdf (p.15, p.20).

No matching passages were provided; general practice.
Uproot and burn heavily infested plants so the grubs inside are destroyed, and replant. Lightly attacked stems can sometimes be saved by cutting below the damage. Smoothen the bark of other stems and maintain good shade.
Documents used: none (general practice).

Trace, uproot and immediately destroy the infested plants by burning, or immerse them under water for a week. If the borer has not reached the root region, the plant can be collar pruned 9-12 inches above the ground and suckers allowed.

**Do today:** Trace infested plants, uproot them and burn them the same day, or keep them under water for 8-10 days; do not store uprooted plants.
**Option:** If the borer has not reached the root system, collar prune 9-12 inches above the ground (not above one foot) and allow suckers.
**Prevent:** Smoothen the main stem and thick primaries with coir gloves and apply 10% lime solution; keep optimum shade; install 25 pheromone traps per hectare where incidence is high.
Documents used: coffee_cultivation_guide.pdf (p.15, p.20, p.27).

25 WSB pheromone traps per hectare should be installed in highly infested areas.

**Traps:** Install 25 white stem borer pheromone traps per hectare where incidence is high; a few traps in strategic places help detect untimely beetle emergence.
**Prevent:** Continue uprooting infested plants, stem smoothening and 10% lime wash, and keep optimum shade.
Documents used: coffee_cultivation_guide.pdf (p.16, p.20).

**Apply:** A 10% lime wash: 10 kg spray lime + 100 ml Fevicol DDL in 100 litres of water, on the main stem and thick primaries.
**Timing:** Smoothen stems in September after the rains, when stems are soft, using coir gloves and without damaging the green parts.
**Prevent:** Install 25 pheromone traps per hectare in highly infested areas.
Documents used: coffee_cultivation_guide.pdf (p.16, p.20, p.27).

Documents used: none (general practice).
Silver oak. Black rot and white stem borer are more prevalent in estates with silver oak as shade tree; mixed shade trees are recommended instead.

**Answer:** Silver oak. Black rot and white stem borer (and leaf rust) are more common in silver-oak-shaded plantations, where soil temperature is higher.
**Prevent:** Plant mixed shade trees instead of silver oak alone: Indian fig, atti, bili basari, mallegargatti, rose wood, jack and leguminous trees; plant shade trees in June-July.
Documents used: coffee_cultivation_guide.pdf (p.56, p.65).

Harvest all ripe berries thoroughly, strip remaining berries at the end of harvest, collect fallen berries (gleaning), dry coffee properly, and use traps; Beauveria bassiana sprays can help.

Use picking mats, pick all left-over berries and gleanings, dip partially damaged berries in boiling water for 1 minute and dry them, burn highly damaged berries, dry coffee to the recommended moisture, do not move coffee from infested areas, and use fumigated or new gunny bags.

**Do today:** Install Broca traps in the estate and near the drying yards; use picking mats during harvest.
**Harvest:** Leave no fruits on the plants after the season: strip the remaining berries and glean fallen ones completely. Dip partially damaged berries in boiling water for 1 minute and dry them; burn highly damaged berries.
**Prevent:** Dry coffee to the recommended moisture, do not move coffee from infested areas, and use clean or fumigated gunny bags.
Documents used: coffee_cultivation_guide.pdf (p.5, p.10, p.13).

**Prevent:** Install Broca traps, use picking mats, strip all remaining berries and glean fallen ones, dry coffee to the recommended moisture and use fumigated or new gunny bags.

Control the ants that spread mealybugs, remove heavily infested parts, and spray a recommended insecticide or neem oil with a wetting agent; release the predator beetle Cryptolaemus where available.

Control the red ants and cocktail ants that spread mealybugs by dusting 5% Malathion powder around the base of affected plants and shade trees and destroying their nests; spray infested plants with Ekalux 25 EC (120 ml) or Metacid 50 EC (120 ml) in 200 litres of water with 200 ml of wetting agent.

**Do today:** Destroy nests of red ants and cocktail ants and dust 5% Malathion powder around the base of affected coffee plants and shade trees.
**Spray:** Ekalux 25 EC (120 ml) or Metacid 50 EC (120 ml) in 200 L of water with 200 ml wetting agent; or 4 L kerosene emulsified in 200 L water with 200 ml wetting agent.
**Timing:** Mealybugs multiply in hot weather after the monsoon and are severe in summer.
**Prevent:** Avoid excessive shade removal; neem kernel extract can also be used.
Documents used: coffee_cultivation_guide.pdf (p.23, Robusta section).

**Timing:** First week of June.
**Prevent:** In black-rot-prone areas thin the overhead shade before the monsoon, centre and handle the bushes, and remove dead branches, suckers and fallen shade-tree leaves from the canopy.

Continuous rain without a dry spell, a saturated atmosphere with 80-100% relative humidity, breeze, thick overhead shade and hanging mist during the monsoon cause the outbreak and spread of black rot.

**Why:** Continuous rain without a dry spell, 80-100% humidity, breeze, thick overhead shade and hanging mist during the monsoon cause black rot; retaining thick shade in the monsoon causes black rot and stalk rot and berry drop because the soil becomes chilly.
**Prevent:** Thin the overhead shade before the monsoon, remove criss-cross and dead branches, and avoid silver-oak monoculture shade.
Documents used: coffee_cultivation_guide.pdf (p.25, p.65).
